previous_non_null_text.title: Head Start and Free School Lunch Elimination - Child Nutrition and Education Access Destruction
previous_non_null_text.description_short: Head Start and Free School Lunch Elimination - Child Nutrition and Education Access Destruction
previous_non_null_text.description_long: Donald Trump implemented Project 2025's systematic destruction of child nutrition and early education by eliminating Head Start programs that served 833,000 children, ending universal free school meals for millions of students, and terminating Community Eligibility Provision programs that provided nutrition security to nearly 20 million students in high-poverty schools. The comprehensive child welfare elimination represented Trump's prioritization of budget cuts over child development, ending programs that provided 'early childhood education, health, nutrition, and parent involvement services to low-income children and families' while creating food insecurity for vulnerable students who relied on school meals for basic nutrition. The systematic program destruction included eliminating Head Start entirely despite serving nearly 40 million children over its history, while ending CEP programs that allowed all students in high-poverty schools to receive free meals without household applications, creating barriers that forced children to 'worry about school lunch or how they're going to pay for their meals.' Trump's child nutrition elimination violated federal obligations to protect vulnerable populations by removing essential support systems that enabled educational success while addressing poverty-related barriers to learning, forcing families to choose between nutrition and other basic needs during economic hardship. The program termination created what child welfare advocates called devastating impact on 'child care deserts' particularly in rural areas where Head Start provided the only early childhood education and nutrition services, while school meal elimination forced children to attend classes hungry and unable to focus on learning. The child welfare destruction represented Project 2025's vision of government that abandoned responsibility for child development and nutrition security, transforming federal budget from tool of social support into mechanism for eliminating programs that had historically reduced educational inequality while providing essential services to America's most vulnerable children and families.

previous_non_null_text.description_long: Donald Trump signed the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act on December 22, 2017; the enacted measure is Public Law 115-97. The law changed both individual and business tax rules. In its 2019 distributional analysis, the Joint Committee on Taxation describes the reduction of the corporate income-tax rate from a graduated structure ranging from 15 percent to 35 percent to a flat 21 percent. It also describes a temporary deduction for qualified business income. The JCT report compares the act’s distributional effects with the law in effect before enactment and provides separate analysis of business-tax provisions. These are concrete provisions that can be described from the statute and JCT analysis. The sources do not justify the prior short description’s broad characterization that benefits were “skewed” toward corporations and high-income earners without identifying a particular year, measure, and distributional table. This entry therefore states the signing date and selected statutory changes, while leaving broader distributional conclusions to a clearly specified analysis rather than treating them as self-evident.

replacement_fields.description_long: The Atlantic’s January 2019 “Unthinkable” project surveyed Donald Trump’s first two years in office through a ranked list of 50 incidents. The page says the editors began with hundreds of moments and selected incidents they considered improbable, norm-bending and destructive; it describes the ranking as subjective and based on both outlandishness and importance. Its entries include Trump praising a congressman who had body-slammed a reporter, a secretary of state’s ouster by tweet, and the first president to complain about an election he had won.
